title: Amazon Cognito & Application Authorization
summary: Sign-up, sign-in and token-based authorization for web, mobile and API users.
tldr: **User pool** = who you are: sign-up, sign-in, social/SAML federation, MFA, and JWTs. **Identity pool** = what AWS you can touch: swaps a token for temporary IAM credentials.

Mobile app writes straight to S3 or DynamoDB? User pool to sign in, identity pool for credentials, and a policy variable like `${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}` to fence each user to their own data.
Machine-to-machine API access uses the **OAuth 2.0 client credentials** grant with custom scopes on a user pool resource server.
Complex business rules (doctor sees only their clinic's patients) belong in **Amazon Verified Permissions** with Cedar policies.

keyFacts.text: Identity pools can issue credentials to **unauthenticated** users through a separate, tightly scoped IAM role, e.g. analytics events before sign-in.
`dynamodb:LeadingKeys` equal to the Cognito identity ID limits each user to items with their own partition key.
**Threat protection** (formerly advanced security) in the Plus feature plan blocks compromised credentials and adds adaptive, risk-based MFA.
Map user pool **groups** to IAM roles and let the identity pool choose the role from the token, so the app can't pick its own permissions.

traps: A user pool token **cannot** call AWS services such as Kinesis or S3 directly; you need an identity pool for IAM credentials.
API keys identify a client for throttling; they are not an authentication mechanism.
GuardDuty doesn't detect or block compromised Cognito passwords; Cognito threat protection does.
A WAF rate-based rule can't spot leaked passwords used slowly; it complements, but doesn't replace, Cognito threat protection.
Letting the app choose the identity pool or role by tier stored on the device is insecure; derive the role from the token.
